title: RBI's Special FCNR Deposit Window Offers NRIs Higher Returns Before September Deadline
excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India's concessional swap facility has pushed FCNR(B) deposit rates to 6-7% for NRIs, with banks racing to attract up to $50 billion in fresh foreign currency inflows before the September 30 cutoff.
body:
• RBI launched a special FCNR(B) deposit framework on June 8, 2026, allowing banks to offer rates of 6-7% on USD deposits — double the previous 3% levels
  • The central bank is absorbing full hedging costs through a concessional swap facility, with the deposit collection window open until September 30, 2026
  • Banks expect $35-50 billion in fresh inflows; net FCNR(B) deposits had collapsed 86% to just $946 million in FY26 from $7.1 billion in FY25
  • Deposits carry a mandatory one-year lock-in period, with 3-5 year tenures, and remain denominated in foreign currency — shielding NRIs from rupee depreciation risk

The Reserve Bank of India is making its most aggressive push in over a decade to draw foreign currency deposits from Non-Resident Indians, with a special FCNR(B) deposit scheme that has more than doubled interest rates and put banks on a sprint to collect billions before the window closes on September 30.

How the Scheme Works

Under the framework launched on June 8, the RBI is offering banks a concessional foreign exchange swap at par — effectively absorbing the full cost of hedging currency risk on fresh 3-to-5-year FCNR(B) deposits. Banks sell their collected dollars to the RBI and receive rupees, with a guaranteed buy-back at the same exchange rate at maturity.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=q-pl0DW6WmY

That zero-cost hedge is the key mechanism. Normally, banks spend heavily to protect against rupee depreciation over a multi-year deposit term, and that cost eats into the rates they can offer depositors. With the RBI bearing that burden, banks have pushed USD deposit rates from around 3% to 6-7% — competitive with and in some cases exceeding U.S. Treasury yields.

"It is a win-win situation for non-resident Indians and for the banks."

— Ashok Chandra, CEO, Punjab National Bank

On June 17, the RBI went further, temporarily removing the interest rate ceiling on fresh FCNR(B) deposits of 3-5 year tenures entirely, giving banks complete flexibility to set competitive rates through September 30.

The Numbers Behind the Push

The urgency is clear from the data. Net FCNR(B) inflows plunged 86% in FY26, falling to just $946 million from $7.1 billion the previous year. Outstanding deposits stood at $33.8 billion at the end of March 2026.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2088272252328648999

Punjab National Bank expects the banking sector to raise $35-40 billion through the scheme. SBI economists project $40-45 billion. Some estimates put the upper bound at $50-70 billion. PNB alone targets $2.5-3 billion and plans to market the deposits aggressively across the U.S., Canada, the U.K., and the Middle East.

The scheme echoes a similar window the RBI opened in 2013, when India faced a currency crisis. That earlier effort successfully attracted over $34 billion in FCNR(B) deposits, stabilizing the rupee and rebuilding forex reserves.

What NRIs Need to Know

The deposits carry a mandatory one-year lock-in — no premature withdrawal is allowed in the first year. After that, some banks like HDFC Bank offer penalty-free early withdrawal, while others may charge up to 1% for premature closure.

FCNR(B) deposits remain denominated in foreign currency throughout their term. At maturity, both principal and interest are paid in the original currency, eliminating rupee exchange-rate risk for depositors. Interest income is also tax-exempt under Indian income tax rules.

Deposits can be opened in USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, CAD, AUD, and SGD, though the RBI's swap facility is available only in U.S. dollars. The minimum tenure under the special window is three years, and the maximum is five.

Strategic Context

The scheme is part of a broader RBI effort to stabilize the rupee and shore up India's foreign exchange reserves. By channeling NRI savings into the formal banking system, the central bank gains a stable source of dollar liquidity that doesn't carry the volatility of portfolio investment flows.

For NRIs weighing the decision, the calculus is straightforward: rates meaningfully above U.S. Treasuries, no currency conversion risk, tax-exempt interest, and full repatriability. The trade-off is the one-year lock-in and a 3-5 year commitment. With the deposit collection window closing September 30 and the swap facility shutting October 16, the timeline to act is narrowing.
